headline_en: PM's Malaysia visit opens new prospects for future cooperation between the two countries: Mahdi Amin
summary_en: On his first foreign visit as Prime Minister, Tarique Rahman met Malaysian PM Anwar Ibrahim on 22 June 2026 and called for the Malaysian labour market to be reopened quickly to Bangladeshi workers, with lower migration cost and safe workplaces. The two sides also discussed regularising or safely returning irregular and jailed Bangladeshis in Malaysia. A 33-point joint statement on nine areas of cooperation was issued.

facts.statement: As of 22 June 2026 the Malaysian labour market was not open to Bangladeshi workers: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, visiting Malaysia, called on Malaysia to quickly reopen ('quickly open up') its labour market for Bangladeshi workers.
facts.source_in_article: Mahdi Amin, adviser to the Prime Minister and spokesperson of the Prime Minister's Office, at a press conference at the Shangri-La hotel in Malaysia on 22 June 2026

facts.statement: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman asked Malaysia to create employment opportunities for more Bangladeshi workers at low cost and through a transparent process, and called for lower migration cost and a safe working environment.
facts.source_in_article: Mahdi Amin, adviser to the Prime Minister and spokesperson of the Prime Minister's Office, at a press conference at the Shangri-La hotel in Malaysia on 22 June 2026

facts.statement: At the Bangladesh-Malaysia prime ministers' meeting on 22 June 2026 the two sides discussed humanely regularising (giving legal status to) Bangladeshis who are in irregular status or in prison in Malaysia, or returning them safely to Bangladesh. The article reports discussion only, not a decision.
facts.source_in_article: Mahdi Amin, adviser to the Prime Minister and spokesperson of the Prime Minister's Office, at a press conference at the Shangri-La hotel in Malaysia on 22 June 2026

facts.statement: Tarique Rahman's visit to Malaysia was his first foreign trip since taking office and lasted about 18 hours; he met Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim (first one-to-one, then at delegation level) and the King, Sultan Ibrahim Sultan Iskandar.
facts.source_in_article: Mahdi Amin, adviser to the Prime Minister and spokesperson of the Prime Minister's Office, at a press conference at the Shangri-La hotel in Malaysia on 22 June 2026

facts.statement: The Bangladesh-Malaysia talks covered political cooperation, trade and investment, halal industry, digital economy, artificial intelligence, semiconductors, the labour market, education, tourism, energy, defence and security; a 33-point joint statement was issued to increase cooperation on nine subjects.
facts.source_in_article: Mahdi Amin, adviser to the Prime Minister and spokesperson of the Prime Minister's Office, at a press conference at the Shangri-La hotel in Malaysia on 22 June 2026

facts.statement: After arriving in Kuala Lumpur, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman held an exchange of views with expatriate Bangladeshis, presented his plans for Bangladesh and recalled expatriates' contribution to the country's development.
facts.source_in_article: Mahdi Amin, adviser to the Prime Minister and spokesperson of the Prime Minister's Office, at a press conference at the Shangri-La hotel in Malaysia on 22 June 2026

facts.statement: Bangladesh and Malaysia agreed to take forward talks on a free trade agreement (FTA), and discussed Malaysian investment in Bangladesh's technology parks and economic zones and cooperation on halal certification, research, training and creating skilled manpower.
facts.source_in_article: Mahdi Amin, adviser to the Prime Minister and spokesperson of the Prime Minister's Office, at a press conference at the Shangri-La hotel in Malaysia on 22 June 2026

facts.statement: During the visit one memorandum of understanding on culture was signed and two 'exchange of notes' (on increasing investment and on counter-terrorism) were exchanged; Bangladesh sought Malaysia's support on Rohingya repatriation, on becoming an ASEAN sectoral dialogue partner and on joining RCEP. Top officials of Petronas, Axiata, AirAsia, Perodua and MMC Port met the Prime Minister.
facts.source_in_article: Mahdi Amin, adviser to the Prime Minister and spokesperson of the Prime Minister's Office, at a press conference at the Shangri-La hotel in Malaysia on 22 June 2026

headline_en: Five young men from Sylhet killed in road accident in Qatar
summary_en: Five Bangladeshi workers from Kanaighat upazila, Sylhet, died on the morning of 21 June 2026 in the Sanaiya area of Qatar when the pickup van taking them to work went out of control. The State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare said the labour wing of the Bangladesh embassy in Qatar has been instructed to bring the bodies home quickly and arrange due financial compensation for the families.

facts.statement: Five Bangladeshi workers from Kanaighat upazila, Sylhet, were killed on the spot on the morning of Sunday 21 June 2026 in the Sanaiya area of Qatar when the pickup van carrying them to their workplace went out of control.
facts.source_in_article: Relatives of the dead; death confirmed by Kanaighat UNO Mehedi Hasan Shakil

facts.statement: The five dead in the Qatar accident were named as Mostak Ahmad (30), son of Salim Ullah, and Zubayer Ahmad (30), son of the late Ahsan Ullah, both of Majhtaluk village, Jhingabari union; Jasim Uddin (30), son of Siraj Uddin, of Agtaluk village; Jibal Ahmad (36), son of Abdun Nur, of Amarpur village; and Kadir Ahmad (24), son of Bahar Uddin, of Gachhbari Noyagram, Dakshin Banigram union, all in Kanaighat upazila, Sylhet.
facts.source_in_article: Abdul Latif, member of Jhingabari Union Parishad

facts.statement: The bodies of the five Bangladeshis killed in the Qatar road accident were kept in the morgue of a local hospital in Qatar; families in Bangladesh learned of the deaths at about 12 noon the same day.
facts.source_in_article: Relatives

facts.statement: The Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment instructed the labour wing of the Bangladesh embassy in Qatar to work with the highest priority to bring the five bodies home quickly and to provide due financial compensation to the affected families. No amount is stated.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister Md. Nurul Haque, in a condolence message

headline_en: Shakil wanted release from a Saudi jail; he came home a lifeless body
summary_en: The body of Shakil Mia (28) of Kishoreganj, who died in a Saudi prison on 15 May 2026, reached his home on 13 June 2026, 28 days after his death, brought back at government initiative. He had gone to Saudi Arabia in 2019 through a Banani recruiting agency, left his employer over an iqama problem, was arrested while working illegally, and the family sent about BDT 180,000 to a lawyer for bail before he died.

facts.statement: Shakil Mia of Kishoreganj went to Saudi Arabia in 2019, on borrowed money, through Altab Recruiting Agency (আলতাব রিক্রুটিং এজেন্সি) in the Banani area of Dhaka.
facts.source_in_article: Bakul Mia, uncle of the deceased

facts.statement: In Saudi Arabia Shakil Mia left his workplace because of complications with his employer over his work/residence permit (iqama); he was later caught by Saudi police while working illegally and sent to prison.
facts.source_in_article: Bakul Mia, uncle of the deceased

facts.statement: From a Saudi prison Shakil Mia told his family that about 2 lakh taka was needed to arrange bail so he could return home; his father says he borrowed and sent about BDT 180,000 to a lawyer in Saudi Arabia. The article gives both figures (about 2 lakh needed; about 1 lakh 80 thousand sent).
facts.source_in_article: Bakul Mia (uncle) and Omar Faruk (father)

facts.statement: Shakil Mia (28) died on 15 May 2026 in a Saudi prison; relatives claim an air conditioner exploded in the prison, creating smoke, and he developed breathing difficulty and died there. He had earlier told family by phone that he was weak, had lost weight and could not eat the prison food.
facts.source_in_article: Relatives' claim

facts.statement: The father of a Bangladeshi who died in a Saudi prison said about 8,000 Saudi riyals were needed to bring the body from Saudi Arabia to Bangladesh, which the family did not have.
facts.source_in_article: Omar Faruk, father of the deceased

facts.statement: Shakil Mia's body was brought home at government initiative after Shariful Alam, MP for Kishoreganj-6 (Bhairab-Kuliarchar) and State Minister for Textiles and Jute, took it up; the body arrived on a Bangladesh Biman flight from Saudi Arabia at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, at about midnight on Friday 12 June 2026 and reached the home in Purba Katiarchar, Maria union, Kishoreganj Sadar, on the morning of 13 June, 28 days after the death.
facts.source_in_article: Family sources; Omar Faruk

facts.statement: Shakil Mia was his family's only earner; the family last spoke to him 10 days before his death, when he asked for money for bail and legal process.

headline_en: India tries to push alleged undocumented Bangladeshis across the border; panic among Muslims in West Bengal
summary_en: An Al Jazeera feature reports that the newly elected BJP government of West Bengal has since late May 2026 been detaining alleged undocumented Bangladeshi Muslim migrants and trying to push them into Bangladesh under a 'detect, delete and deport' policy, with temporary detention centres in every district. Bangladeshi families who had crossed with brokers to work in Kolkata describe surrendering or leaving out of fear. Dhaka has protested and BGB says it blocked at least 18 push-in attempts since 4 June.

facts.statement: In late May 2026 West Bengal's newly elected BJP chief minister Suvendu Adhikari ordered alleged Bangladeshi migrants living illegally in the state to be sent back, under a state 'detect, delete and deport' policy; the state also announced building 'holding centres' to detain alleged illegal Bangladeshis before return. The BJP had come to power in West Bengal for the first time about a month before mid-June 2026.
facts.source_in_article: Al Jazeera report carried by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari said the drive would be conducted only against Muslim Bangladeshis; Hindu and other-faith migrants are excluded under a disputed constitutional amendment (as the article words it). He also said detainees need not be taken to court before expulsion.
facts.source_in_article: Al Jazeera report carried by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: In December 2025 India's Supreme Court ruled that foreign nationals have almost no rights under the Indian constitution; as a result, under the West Bengal policy people facing expulsion have to prove why they should not be sent to Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: Al Jazeera report carried by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: In the two weeks to about 13 June 2026 thousands of people were detained across West Bengal; some were sent to detention centres and others taken to the border in attempts to push them into Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: Al Jazeera report carried by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: On Sunday 7 June 2026 West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari claimed about 5,000 Bangladeshi nationals had already been sent back; in his own words 4,800 'Bangladeshi infiltrators' had been returned from the centres and 836 more were in detention centres awaiting quick return. He said temporary detention centres had been set up in every district of the state.
facts.source_in_article: Suvendu Adhikari, to journalists in Kolkata

facts.statement: A police officer on duty at Hakimpur border checkpost (North 24 Parganas, about 80 km from Kolkata) claimed 250 to 300 undocumented migrants and refugees arrive there (are brought to the border detention centre) every day; their citizenship is checked and biometric data collected to build a digital list of migrants. Crowds have been seen at Hakimpur and other West Bengal border posts since late May 2026.
facts.source_in_article: Unnamed police officer at Hakimpur, to Al Jazeera

facts.statement: Raisul Islam (38) of Satkhira said he paid a broker about USD 250 (about BDT 30,700 at the rate given in the article) to get himself and his family across the border into India two years earlier.
facts.source_in_article: Raisul Islam, to Al Jazeera

facts.statement: Raisul Islam and his wife both worked as masons on the outskirts of Kolkata and together earned about USD 10 a day (about BDT 1,230); he said wages in India were higher than what he earned in Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: Raisul Islam, to Al Jazeera

facts.statement: Mirajul Gazi (42) and his wife worked as construction labourers in Kolkata and earned about USD 12 a day (about BDT 1,470).
facts.source_in_article: Mirajul Gazi, to Al Jazeera

facts.statement: Raisul Islam said he and his family surrendered voluntarily before the authorities found them, fearing harassment by local people and police as illegal migrants; Indian security forces then took his family by vehicle to a detention centre 18 km from Hakimpur checkpost.
facts.source_in_article: Raisul Islam; Al Jazeera reporter

facts.statement: Mirajul Gazi said he had no problem for five years in Kolkata, but after the new government came to power his landlord told him to leave, and fearing attack by locals the family decided to return to Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: Mirajul Gazi, to Al Jazeera

facts.statement: Many migrants gathered at Hakimpur said economic hardship and lack of livelihood in Bangladesh forced them to cross the border into India with the help of brokers; many had no valid papers.
facts.source_in_article: Migrants at Hakimpur, to Al Jazeera

facts.statement: Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) said that since 4 June 2026 it had blocked at least 18 'push-in' attempts by India's BSF, in which about 180 people were to be pushed into Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: BGB

facts.statement: Bangladesh's State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed said at a Dhaka press conference (Monday, about 8 June 2026) that Dhaka had sent '12 to 13 letters' to Delhi on the matter, that there is a set mechanism for verifying nationality of undocumented migrants which Indian authorities must follow, and that the drive could affect bilateral relations.
facts.source_in_article: Shama Obaed

facts.statement: At the 57th BGB-BSF director-general-level border conference in Delhi (started Monday, ended Thursday, about 8-11 June 2026) BGB called for an end to 'push-ins' into Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: Al Jazeera report carried by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: India's foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal claimed illegal foreigners are being dealt with under Indian law, that Bangladesh and other countries were informed for verification, and that many such requests are still pending verification by Dhaka; according to media reports India's foreign ministry has sent details of more than 2,800 suspected Bangladeshis to Dhaka.
facts.source_in_article: Randhir Jaiswal; various media

facts.statement: In summer 2025 Indian security agencies in Assam accused about 12 Indian Muslims of being undocumented migrants and forced them across the border into Bangladesh; Bangladesh sent them back, they were stranded for a time in no man's land and were finally taken back into India, without explanation or redress.
facts.source_in_article: Al Jazeera report carried by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Human Rights Watch Asia director Elaine Pearson said detainees should have the right to legal aid even without valid papers, so that no Indian citizen is wrongly expelled, and called the process 'illegal'. Activist Teesta Setalvad said police are indiscriminately picking people up and sending them to detention centres and demanded full disclosure of data on those detained and expelled.
facts.source_in_article: Elaine Pearson (HRW) and Teesta Setalvad, to Al Jazeera

facts.statement: Bangladesh and India share a 4,096 km land border; West Bengal has about 100 million people, about 27 percent of them Muslim.
facts.source_in_article: Al Jazeera report carried by Prothom Alo

headline_en: Various facilities announced for the service sector
summary_en: A report on the proposed FY 2026-27 budget's service-sector measures. For migrants, the budget announces a 'Probashi Card' for outbound and working expatriates to store worker data and ease access to government services and welfare benefits, and stresses new labour markets, skills, easy-term loans and safe migration. It also proposes a single ID for all services and a student education loan programme.

facts.statement: The proposed FY 2026-27 budget announces the launch of a 'Probashi Card' (প্রবাসী কার্ড) for people going abroad and expatriates working abroad; through the card, workers' information will be stored and the process of taking various government services and getting welfare benefits will be made easier. No launch date, fee or issuing office is stated.
facts.source_in_article: Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury, proposed budget for FY 2026-27

facts.statement: The proposed FY 2026-27 budget puts emphasis on exploring new labour markets, skills development, loans on easy terms and a safe migration system for migrant workers; the article gives no amounts or terms.
facts.source_in_article: Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury, proposed budget for FY 2026-27

facts.statement: The proposed FY 2026-27 budget seeks to encourage migration, transport and government-service digitalisation through tax and VAT exemptions (no detail given).
facts.source_in_article: Reporter's summary of the budget

facts.statement: The budget proposes a single ID through which all government and private services can be taken, and strengthening Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) so that government services, fee payment, registration and information verification can be done on one digital platform.
facts.source_in_article: Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury, proposed budget for FY 2026-27

facts.statement: The budget proposes an education loan programme for students so that financial limits do not keep anyone from higher education or technical training.
facts.source_in_article: Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury, proposed budget for FY 2026-27

headline_en: Nearly 2.5 billion dollars in remittances came in just 19 days
summary_en: Ahead of Eid-ul-Azha, Bangladeshis abroad sent USD 2,483 million in the first 19 days of May 2026, 38 percent more than the same period a year earlier, according to Bangladesh Bank. Fiscal-year remittances from July to 19 May reached USD 31,816 million, and the central bank is buying surplus dollars from banks.

facts.statement: Remittances to Bangladesh in the first 19 days of May 2026 were USD 248 crore 30 lakh (USD 2,483 million), against USD 179 crore 30 lakh in the same period of the previous year, a rise of 38 percent.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank report

facts.statement: From July of the current fiscal year to 19 May 2026, Bangladesh received USD 3,181 crore 60 lakh (USD 31,816 million) in remittances.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank report

facts.statement: Bank officials said expatriates were sending more money ahead of Eid-ul-Azha (Qurbani Eid) and that at this pace May 2026 remittances could exceed USD 3 billion before Eid.
facts.source_in_article: Bank officials

facts.statement: Because higher remittances created a dollar surplus in banks, Bangladesh Bank has been buying dollars to build reserves; on 20 May 2026 it bought USD 7 crore from four banks at BDT 122.75 per dollar.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank report

headline_en: Canada's Post-Graduation Work Permit: the 10 mistakes that get applications refused
summary_en: An explainer on Canada's Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP), an open work permit of up to three years for graduates of Canadian institutions, listing ten reasons applications are refused after recent IRCC rule changes. It covers eligible programmes (CIP list), full-time status, the 24-hour off-campus work limit, in-Canada study, language scores, the 180-day deadline, documents, passport validity, temporary intent and inadmissibility.

facts.statement: Canada's Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) is an open work permit that lets graduates of Canadian educational institutions work for any employer in Canada; depending on the length of study it can be valid for up to three years.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

facts.statement: Since 2024 only programmes on the IRCC-approved Classification of Instructional Programs (CIP) list are eligible for the PGWP. Recently 119 new fields were added and 178 programmes removed, effective from the start of 2026. Diploma and certificate students in particular must confirm their programme's CIP code; changing programme midway means eligibility must be re-checked under the new code.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

facts.statement: For the PGWP a student must keep full-time enrolment throughout the study period; part-time is allowed only in the final semester, and part-time study at other times can make the application ineligible.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

facts.statement: International students in Canada may currently work off-campus up to 24 hours a week while classes are in session; working without authorisation can cancel student status and lead to PGWP refusal.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

facts.statement: Online study from outside Canada counted towards PGWP eligibility during Covid, but this no longer applies to programmes that started after September 2024; study must now be completed while present in Canada.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

facts.statement: From 1 November 2024 proof of language proficiency is mandatory for the PGWP: minimum CLB 5 for college graduates and CLB 7 for bachelor's, master's or PhD graduates; test results more than two years old are not accepted.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

facts.statement: A PGWP application must be submitted within 180 days of receiving proof of programme completion; after the deadline the application is generally refused.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

facts.statement: The PGWP is applied for online. Required documents: proof of programme completion (degree, diploma or transcript), proof of full-time enrolment, language test results, proof of an eligible programme and, if required, medical exam results. Incomplete applications are refused.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

facts.statement: A PGWP cannot be valid beyond the passport's expiry; if the passport expires earlier the work permit is issued for a shorter time, so it is better to renew the passport before applying.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

facts.statement: A PGWP applicant must show they will leave Canada when the permit ends (temporary intent), even if they may later wish to settle; family ties, property or proof of a job in the home country help.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

facts.statement: A person can be found inadmissible to Canada for medical problems, insufficient financial means, a criminal record, security risk or giving false information; even a family member's inadmissibility can affect the application.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules
